Franciscan
fran-SIS-kun
n. and a. (a member of the Order of Friars Minor founded by Francis of Assisi in 1209; of that order)
From Francis (Latin Franciscus) of Assisi; the order's own name was Ordo Fratrum Minorum, the Order of Lesser Brothers.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Franciscans are the friars of Francis of Assisi, approved in 1209, who called themselves not the Great but the Lesser Brothers. Their founding texts were taken straight from the gospels: “If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me” (Mat 19:21), and the charge to the Twelve, “Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money” (Luk 9:3). Francis read these as a literal rule of life, and the order he left preached barefoot, worked among lepers, and refused property corporately as well as individually. A Protestant must say two things about it. First, the movement recovered real neglected scripture — the gospel preached to the poor, a ministry not for gain, a church visibly unattached to money — and it shamed a wealthy hierarchy by simply obeying. Second, it mistook a commission for a counsel and a means for a merit. Poverty is not holiness; Christ's word to the rich young man exposed an idol in that particular man, and “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith” (Jam 2:5) speaks of God's election, not of poverty earning anything.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Franciscan as belonging to the order of St Francis, and as a noun one of the order of St Francis, called also Gray Friars and Minorites; and mendicant as one of the begging fraternities of the Romish church.

expand to see more

FRANCISCAN, a. Belonging to the order of St. Francis.

FRANCISCAN, n. One of the order of St. Francis; an order of religious, called also Gray Friars, and Minorites.

MINOR, a. Less; smaller; inferior; as the minor part of the society.

POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.

PERFECT, a. Finished; complete; consummate; not defective; having all that is requisite to its nature and kind.

Key Scripture

Mat 19:21 — "Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me."

Luk 9:3 — "And he said unto them, Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece."

Jam 2:5 — "Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?"

Luk 12:33 — "Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth."

Modern Corruption

The Friars Minor of Francis of Assisi: a genuine recovery of the gospel preached to the poor, built on a vow that treated poverty itself as merit.

expand to see more

The doctrinal corruption is the merit of poverty, and it is not a small thing. If selling all is the counsel of perfection, then there are two grades of Christian and the gospel has a higher tier for the heroic. Scripture refuses that division. Paul, who knew real destitution — “in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness” (2Co 11:27) — never once counts it toward his standing, and declares his contentment learnt in both conditions: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Phi 4:12).

The modern misuse of Francis is to keep him as a sentimental figure of birds and ecology and to drop the Christ he preached. That is a far worse corruption than his vow was. The principle to recover is the one he genuinely saw: a church attached to money cannot preach to the poor, and “Sell that ye have, and give alms” (Luk 12:33) is addressed to disciples who had a great deal more to give than they thought.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin minor, lesser; Greek ptochos (G4434), poor; Greek teleios (G5046), complete or perfect; Greek akoloutheo (G190), to follow; Hebrew ani (H6041), afflicted or poor.

expand to see more

Latin fratres minores — lesser brothers; the order's own chosen name, and a rebuke to rank.

Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, mature; “If thou wilt be perfect” (Mat 19:21) — wholeness, not a higher tier.

Greek akoloutheo (G190) — to follow, to accompany as a disciple; the verb of the call.

Greek ptochos (G4434) — the destitute poor, those to whom the gospel is preached.

Hebrew ani (H6041) — poor, afflicted, bowed down; the Psalter's word for the man God hears.

Usage

"“go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mat 19:21) — the text Francis read as a rule for all."

"“Take nothing for your journey” (Luk 9:3) — a commission for a mission, taken as a permanent vow."

"“I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Phi 4:12) — Paul's verdict on both estates."
